questions.question: When GHC type-checks `'a' == 'b'`, how does it decide which == to run?
options: It tries every available Eq instance at run time until one works
It infers the type of the operands at compile time (here Char) and uses that type's Eq instance
It always uses the Eq Integer instance and converts everything to a number first
== has one single global implementation shared by every type
questions.explanation: Dispatch happens once, at compile time, based on the inferred type of the arguments. 'a' and 'b' are Chars, so the Eq Char instance's == is the one compiled into the program — there is no run-time searching.
optionFeedback: There is no run-time trial-and-error; the type is known at compile time, and exactly one instance's implementation is selected then.
Correct — the type Char is inferred first, and the Eq Char instance supplies the specific == that gets compiled in.
Char values are not converted to Integer for comparison; each type has its own independent Eq instance and its own comparison logic.
This is precisely what overloading denies — == has a different implementation per instance, selected by type, not one shared implementation.

questions.question: Why is countMatches3 :: a -> [a] -> Int (fully general, no constraint) not just 'too general' but actually impossible to write?
options: It would need to be much longer than the other two versions
Counting matches means comparing the target to each element with ==, and an unconstrained a supports no operations at all — the body cannot even type-check, let alone run
Int cannot be returned from a fully general function
It is possible, but only for list arguments of length 1
questions.explanation: This goes one step further than the usual 'too narrow / too general' trade-off: countMatches3's body has no way to compare v to an element of the list at all, because == requires Eq, which the signature never grants. It fails to compile for any input, not just some.
optionFeedback: Length has nothing to do with it — countMatches2's body, length . filter (== v), is no longer than a countMatches3 body would be if one could be written at all.
Correct — comparing v against each element needs ==, and Eq a => is the constraint that makes == available; without it, the comparison itself cannot be typed.
Returning Int is fine for any signature shape; the problem is entirely on the input side, not the result type.
The failure is a type error at compile time, for every input, regardless of the list's length — it is not a special case for short lists.

questions.question: showAll :: (Show a, Ord a) => [a] -> String earns both of its constraints honestly. Which operation in its body needs which constraint?
options: maximum needs Show; the two show calls need Ord
maximum needs Ord (to compare elements and find the largest); the two show calls need Show (to convert values to text)
Both constraints are needed only for the ++ that joins the strings together
Neither constraint is actually required; they were added out of caution
questions.explanation: showAll xs = show (maximum xs) ++ " is the largest of " ++ show xs calls maximum, which requires Ord to compare elements, and show, which requires Show to produce text. Each constraint traces to a specific operation in the body, exactly as Section 5 describes GHC inferring them.
optionFeedback: This has the two constraints swapped — maximum is the one that compares elements (Ord), and show is the one that converts to text (Show).
Correct — maximum's comparison needs Ord, and both show calls need Show; the signature states exactly what the body actually uses, no more.
++ on String needs no class constraint at all; String already supports it unconditionally, so ++ contributes nothing to the tuple of constraints.
Both are load-bearing: drop either one and the corresponding operation (maximum or show) fails to type-check.

questions.question: GHC reports `No instance for (Eq a) arising from a use of '=='` inside the body of a function you wrote. What is the repair?
options: Add deriving (Eq) to some data declaration
Add Eq a => to your function's own type signature
Rename the type variable from a to something else
Remove the == from the function body
questions.explanation: The class named in lowercase (a) is a type variable from your own signature, not a fixed type. The repair is to state, in that signature, that a must belong to Eq — exactly the countOf repair shown in this section.
optionFeedback: There is no concrete data type named here to add a deriving clause to — the problem is an unconstrained variable in a signature you wrote.
Correct — a is your function's own type variable; adding Eq a => to its signature states the requirement that == already relies on.
The variable's name is irrelevant; whatever it is called, it still needs the constraint added.
The == is exactly what the function is meant to do; removing it would just produce a different, wrong function.

questions.question: GHC reports `No instance for (Eq Direction) arising from a use of '=='`, where Direction is a data type you declared with no deriving clause. What is the repair?
options: Add Eq a => to the signature of the function that used ==
Add deriving (Eq) to the Direction declaration, or write an Eq Direction instance by hand
Rename Direction to a lowercase name
Direction cannot be compared under any circumstances
questions.explanation: Direction is a concrete type, not a variable — there is no signature constraint to add. The instance itself is missing for this specific type, so it must be supplied, most easily by deriving it.
optionFeedback: There is no type variable here to constrain; Direction is already a fixed, concrete type named directly in the error.
Correct — the fix supplies the missing Eq Direction instance directly, either via deriving or a hand-written instance declaration.
Capitalisation marks Direction as a concrete type, not a variable; renaming it would not create the missing instance and would break every other use of the type.
It can be compared perfectly well once it has an Eq instance — deriving (Eq) is enough, as the corrected declaration shows.

questions.question: Why does `countMax :: Ord a => [a] -> Int` type-check, even though its body uses ==, which belongs to Eq?
options: == is defined inside every class, not just Eq
Ord requires Eq as a superclass, so every Ord instance is guaranteed to already be an Eq instance
GHC silently adds Eq a => whenever it sees ==
countMax does not actually use == at compile time
questions.explanation: Because Ord's own class definition requires Eq, any type with an Ord instance is guaranteed to have an Eq instance too. The Ord a constraint already carries that guarantee, so == is available without writing Eq a separately.
optionFeedback: == belongs specifically to Eq; other classes such as Ord add their own new operations (<, compare, ...) on top of it, rather than redefining it.
Correct — the Eq -> Ord arrow in the hierarchy means Ord a already implies Eq a, so == is available for free.
Nothing is added silently; the guarantee comes from Ord's fixed definition (it requires Eq), not from any special-casing of ==.
filter (== maximum xs) xs genuinely calls == at run time on every element; it is a real, executed comparison, not something erased.

questions.question: Why is writing `(Eq a, Ord a) => ...` considered redundant rather than merely allowed?
options: It is a syntax error in Haskell
Because Ord a already guarantees Eq a, so naming Eq a separately adds no new information
Because Eq and Ord are actually the same class under different names
Because a can only ever belong to one class at a time
questions.explanation: It compiles fine — it is just unnecessary. Ord's definition already requires Eq, so any type satisfying Ord a satisfies Eq a automatically; spelling out both says nothing the single Ord a did not already say.
optionFeedback: It is valid, if wordy, Haskell — GHC accepts it without complaint. The issue is that it says the same thing twice.
Correct — since Ord requires Eq as a superclass, Ord a on its own already entails Eq a, making the explicit Eq a superfluous.
They are distinct classes providing different operations (== and /= for Eq; <, compare, max, min for Ord, on top of Eq's operations).
A type may satisfy any number of classes simultaneously — Int alone is an instance of Eq, Ord, Num, Show, and more.
